comparison: Perfect agreement on claims C18-C21, C79 regarding 5' UTR translation and uORFs. Both evaluations support these findings without challenge. OpenEval provides detailed technical validation while peer reviewers accept the characterization as part of the ribosome profiling system.

Perfect agreement on claims C28-C34 regarding exclusion of alternative mechanisms (selenocysteine, RNA editing). Both evaluations support the systematic ruling out of these alternatives. OpenEval highlights the rigorous A-site footprint analysis while peer reviewers accept these exclusionary analyses without critique.

Perfect agreement on claims C9, C35-C36, C62-C63 regarding cross-species conservation of readthrough. Both evaluations support the triplet periodicity data and conservation evidence. OpenEval emphasizes this strengthens biological importance while peer reviewers accept it as part of the genome-wide analysis.

Strong disagreement on claims C6, C40-C41, C64-C68 regarding evolutionary selection on novel extensions. OpenEval finds the Z-curve and SNP analyses provide statistically significant support for selection. Peer reviewers find the analysis 'problematic' and state the data are 'equally, if not more, consistent' with weak selection of unknown origin rather than recent evolutionary origin.

Perfect agreement on claims C8, C42-C45, C69-C70 regarding regulated readthrough. Both evaluations support this as an 'important conclusion' demonstrating biological significance. OpenEval validates the statistical approach while peer reviewers explicitly affirm regulation argues for functional importance.

Perfect agreement on claims C7, C46-C50 regarding functional localization signals in extensions. Both evaluations support the experimental validation of NLSes as evidence of functional importance. OpenEval notes some predictions remain untested while peer reviewers accept this as an 'important conclusion' without critique.

Perfect agreement on claims C51-C53 regarding stage-specific readthrough predictions. Both evaluations support these inferences from the regulation data. OpenEval notes these require future validation while peer reviewers accept them as consistent with the regulated readthrough findings.

Perfect agreement on claims C83-C84 regarding quality control for alternative explanations of 3' UTR ribosome density. Both evaluations support the authors' ability to distinguish readthrough from other phenomena. OpenEval emphasizes this strengthens confidence in readthrough calls while peer reviewers implicitly accept this quality control.

Agreement on claims C4-C5, C22-C23 regarding pervasiveness of readthrough beyond phylogenetic predictions. Both evaluations support this as an 'important conclusion.' OpenEval also includes claims C3, C81-C82 about the 307 novel extensions representing a major finding, which peer reviewers affirm without challenge.

Disagreement on claims C24-C26 regarding whether footprints represent actively translating ribosomes. OpenEval finds three independent lines of evidence provide strong support. Peer reviewers raise a 'key concern' about whether ribosomes failed to release properly and request additional RRS analysis, indicating current evidence is insufficient.

Disagreement on claims C37-C39 regarding biological significance thresholds. OpenEval rates as UNCERTAIN due to arbitrary threshold definition but suggests high percentages indicate functionality. Peer reviewers express concern about the 1-3% readthrough levels and question whether this justifies claims of being 'functionally consequential,' requesting clearer presentation of mean readthrough levels.

Disagreement on claims C54, C71 regarding the evolutionary model and functional consequences. OpenEval supports the synthesis as coherent and well-supported by multiple lines of evidence. Peer reviewers state the claims are 'somewhat overstating your results' given 1-3% readthrough levels and note that functional consequence cannot be claimed without phenotypic validation through deletion experiments.

Agreement on claims C10-C12 regarding MNase-based protocol validation. OpenEval supports the technical claims about necessity and reliability. Peer reviewers describe the ribosome profiling assay development as 'thorough, compelling' and accept the technical quality, though R10 also covers additional technical claims C13, C74-C78.

Agreement on claims C14-C17 regarding translational regulation in embryos. OpenEval supports the quantitative measurements showing mRNA predicts only one-third of protein variance. Peer reviewers accept these findings about translational regulation without challenge as part of the ribosome profiling characterization.

Agreement on claims C74-C76 regarding technical validation of ribosome recovery. OpenEval supports the quantitative recovery data (1.04-fold) as demonstrating minimal loss. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the 'thorough, compelling' assay development described in R10.

Agreement on claims C77-C78 regarding assay sensitivity and reproducibility. OpenEval supports the low standard deviation between replicates as enabling detection of modest regulatory changes. Peer reviewers implicitly accept this as part of the overall technical quality affirmed in R10.

Partial overlap on claims C57-C58 regarding readthrough rate quantification. OpenEval supports the quantitative characterization and notes higher rates for conserved extensions. Peer reviewers (R6) express concern about clarity in presenting mean readthrough levels and question whether 1-3% rates justify functional significance claims, though R6 also addresses C37-C39 about biological significance thresholds.

Partial overlap on claim C27 regarding protein product detection. OpenEval supports the IP-western data showing readthrough generates stable proteins in 8/15 reporters, noting the 47% failure rate. Peer reviewers (R5) raise broader concerns about whether ribosomes represent active translation or failed release, requesting RRS analysis, which relates to but extends beyond the protein detection claim.

Peer reviewers ask about triplet periodicity resolution in fly data (C60-C61, C62) and whether MNase bias affects the fly results. No corresponding OpenEval result specifically addresses this methodological question about species-specific resolution differences, though R8 discusses cross-species conservation generally.
